stories.title: Who was Yasser Arafat, and how did Palestinians mark the 22nd anniversary of his death this week?
stories.short: Who was Yasser Arafat?
stories.gist: The PLO chairman and first Palestinian president died on 11 November 2004; a wreath was laid at his Ramallah tomb on Wednesday.
body: Palestinian Vice-President Hussein al-Sheikh laid a wreath at the tomb of Yasser Arafat in the presidential compound in Ramallah on Wednesday 11 November, on behalf of President Mahmoud Abbas, WAFA reported. It was the 22nd anniversary of Arafat's death. Al-Sheikh recited verses from the Quran at the graveside. The ceremony is held every year at the mausoleum inside the compound known as the Muqata'a.

Arafat, known as Abu Ammar, was born in 1929. He was among the founders of the Fatah movement in the late 1950s and became chairman of the Palestine Liberation Organization in February 1969, a post he held until his death. In 1974 he addressed the UN General Assembly, where he spoke of carrying an olive branch and a freedom fighter's gun. In November 1988 the PLO under his leadership declared the State of Palestine.

He signed the Oslo accords with Israel in 1993 and shared the 1994 Nobel Peace Prize with Yitzhak Rabin and Shimon Peres. That year he returned from exile and settled in Gaza City as head of the new Palestinian Authority. The peace process stalled; during the second intifada the Israeli army confined him to his Ramallah compound for more than two years.

He died on 11 November 2004 in a military hospital at Clamart, near Paris, aged 75. The cause has been disputed ever since. Russian and French investigations found no evidence of foul play, while a Swiss team concluded that he had been poisoned with radioactive polonium, according to the summary of the inquiries on Wikipedia. He is buried in a mausoleum inside the compound where he spent his last years.

In a statement the day before the anniversary, Abbas said honouring Arafat meant holding to the principles he died for: self-determination, the return of refugees, and an independent state on the 1967 lines with East Jerusalem as its capital. He referred to Arafat's death as an assassination, the official Palestinian position, and said it had not broken the will of the Palestinian people.

Abbas used the occasion to address present politics. He called national unity an urgent priority, described the PLO as the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people, and urged all factions to end the division under the formula of one authority, one law and one legitimate weapon. He also pledged to press for aid to enter Gaza, for reconstruction and against displacement. Presidential and legislative elections that had been planned were postponed in October, according to a chronology of the year's events.

stories.title: Red Crescent official warns of rising infections in Gaza as sewage mixes with floodwater in camps
stories.short: Red Crescent: infections rising after Gaza floods
stories.gist: The Red Crescent's Bashar Murad says about 70,000 tents were flooded and respiratory infections and meningitis cases are increasing.
body: The Palestine Red Crescent Society's director of health programmes in Gaza, Bashar Murad, warned on Wednesday 11 November that the health situation in the Strip is deteriorating after last week's storm. Speaking to Voice of Palestine radio in remarks carried by WAFA, he said about 70,000 tents had been flooded, affecting tens of thousands of people, and that rainwater mixing with sewage inside displacement camps threatens to spread disease.

Murad said clinics are already seeing more upper respiratory tract infections and more cases of meningitis as temperatures fall and families go without winter clothing or any means of heating. He described a severe shortage of medicines, medical supplies and heating equipment. His warning matches a note in OCHA's storm report that health partners expect higher caseloads and are short of fever medicines, antibiotics and treatments for vomiting and diarrhoea.

Diagnosis is a separate problem. According to Murad there is not a single MRI machine in Gaza and only a limited number of CT scanners. Laboratory solutions and supplies are running short and several laboratories have stopped operating altogether. That leaves doctors unable to run basic tests, he said, which is particularly dangerous for people with chronic illnesses whose treatment depends on regular monitoring, and it puts those patients' lives at risk.

Palestinian Health Minister Majed Abu Ramadan issued an urgent appeal on 7 November as the first tents went under water. He warned that cold, damp and overcrowded shelters raise the risk of influenza and pneumonia among infants, older people and patients, while accumulated waste and sewage contamination encourage rodents and insects and the spread of water-borne infections. Malnutrition, he added, weakens people's ability to fight off illness, especially children and pregnant and breastfeeding women.

The storm damaged the health system directly. OCHA reported water entering departments at Nasser Medical Complex and at facilities run by UK-Med, flooding in a hospital basement that houses paediatric, pharmacy and radiology units, and damage to two clinics and two medical points. Médecins du Monde recorded a 54 per cent drop in consultations because flooded roads kept staff from reaching work. Surveillance has been stepped up for acute watery diarrhoea, respiratory and skin infections and acute jaundice syndrome.

Some outside help was announced this week. On 10 November Japan signed a grant of 294 million yen, about $1.97 million, with the World Health Organization to set up a coordination cell for emergency medical teams inside the health ministry's operations centre in Gaza City and to train and equip 100 local team members. Abu Ramadan called the first rains a serious warning of what further storms could bring to families already at the limit.

stories.title: Settlers set fire to a scrapyard in al-Lubban ash-Sharqiya, burning more than 100 vehicles and olive trees
stories.short: More than 100 vehicles burned in village south of Nablus
stories.gist: WAFA reports that dozens of settlers torched a scrapyard, cars and olive trees in al-Lubban ash-Sharqiya; losses exceed one million shekels.
body: Dozens of Israeli settlers attacked the village of al-Lubban ash-Sharqiya, south of Nablus, and set fire to a vehicle scrapyard, burning more than 100 vehicles, WAFA reported on Wednesday 11 November. The attack took place in the al-Qanater area on the northern edge of the village. The fire also consumed dozens of olive trees and storage buildings, according to the agency's account from the scene.

The flames spread beyond the yard. About 10 cars belonging to residents and parked beside their homes were burned, along with several vehicles at a nearby repair workshop. Street-light poles caught fire, cutting electricity to the area. The head of the village council told WAFA that losses were estimated at more than one million shekels, a figure that has not been independently assessed.

Hundreds of residents tried to hold the fire back with basic tools before firefighters arrived. Five Civil Defense crews, from Salfit, Aqraba, Burin, Sinjil and Abwein, then worked for more than five hours to put it out. Several people suffered from smoke inhalation from the burning vehicles and were treated on the spot by Palestine Red Crescent teams from Salfit working with the village's own volunteers.

WAFA said more than 10 Israeli military vehicles entered the village and drove towards the site of the fire. The report does not mention any arrests. There was no immediate public comment from the Israeli military in the reports seen by this newspaper, and the identity of the attackers has not been established beyond the description given by residents and local officials.

Al-Lubban ash-Sharqiya sits beside Route 60, the main north-south road through the West Bank, and close to several settlements. The attack fits a pattern documented by the UN: OCHA recorded 457 settler attacks causing casualties or damage across the West Bank in October, the highest monthly total since it began keeping records in 2006. Two days earlier, WAFA reported, settlers set fire to heavy machinery and vehicles at an industrial zone south of Nablus.

The Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission, a Palestinian Authority body, says Nablus governorate has seen more attacks on farmers this olive season than any other, 230 between 1 October and 6 November. The commission and UN human rights officials have repeatedly said that such attacks are rarely prosecuted. UN Secretary-General António Guterres, speaking in Antalya on 10 November, called the situation in the West Bank absolutely unacceptable.

stories.title: London Palestine Film Festival opens Friday with 27 screenings, from Gaza testimony to a Jenin projectionist
stories.short: London Palestine Film Festival opens at the Barbican
stories.gist: The festival runs 13-27 November across London venues, opening at the Barbican with the UK premiere of 'Who Is Still Alive'.
body: The London Palestine Film Festival opens on Friday 13 November at the Barbican with the UK premiere of 'Who Is Still Alive', a documentary by the Swiss director Nicolas Wadimoff built from the accounts of nine people who escaped the destruction of Gaza. The film is Switzerland's submission for the 2027 Academy Awards, according to the Barbican's programme. The opening-night screening, which is followed by a discussion, was listed as sold out; a second screening is scheduled for Saturday afternoon.

The festival runs until 27 November. Its website lists more than 27 screenings at venues including the Barbican, the Institute of Contemporary Arts, Cine Lumière, the Rio Cinema, Riverside Studios, the Garden Cinema, Bertha DocHouse and three Curzon cinemas, with one event at the Ropetackle Arts Centre in Shoreham, West Sussex. The organisers, a community interest company, describe their aim as bringing filmmakers, scholars and the public together around Palestinian cinema, culture and politics.

At the Barbican, the week's programme moves from Gaza to the West Bank and Lebanon. 'From Ground Zero+', on 16 November, gathers five short films from Gaza, three of them UK premieres. 'Habibi Hussein', the first feature by Alex Bakri, on 18 November, follows the last projectionist of the old cinema in Jenin as he tries to keep his craft alive. Lana Daher's 'Do You Love Me', made entirely from archive footage of Beirut, screens on 19 November.

Elsewhere the programme ranges widely. 'Who Killed Alex Odeh?', having its UK premiere at the ICA, revisits the 1985 killing of a Palestinian American community leader in California. 'A Man Fell' is set in the former Gaza Hospital building in Sabra, Beirut, now home to a refugee community. 'Life Support' follows foreign doctors working in Gaza, and 'Madleens' looks at the flotilla movement of the same name. There is also a documentary on the life of Edward Said.

The festival pays tribute this year to Mohammad Bakri, the Palestinian actor and director who died in 2025, with screenings at the Rio Cinema on 19 November and at Riverside Studios on 20 November. Maha Haj's 2022 comedy-drama 'Mediterranean Fever' is also on the bill. The closing film, at Curzon Mayfair on 27 November, is 'Conversation with the Sea', about a Palestinian father ordered to pay a social security debt left by his son, who drowned in the Red Sea.

London is not the only British city with a Palestinian film season this month; Leeds holds its own festival from 13 November. For the Palestinian community in Britain the London event is an annual meeting point. For filmmakers in Gaza, where the UN's special rapporteur said in October that about 150 media centres and offices have been destroyed, a festival screening abroad is one of the ways new work still reaches an audience.

stories.title: Qalqilya residents rally in hospital courtyard against UNRWA plan to close the 63-bed facility
stories.short: Qalqilya protests plan to close UNRWA hospital
stories.gist: Protesters want UNRWA to keep its Qalqilya hospital, open since 1951 and serving more than 17,000 refugee families, and reopen two wards.
body: Officials, refugee committee members and residents gathered on Tuesday 10 November in the courtyard of the UNRWA hospital in Qalqilya to protest against the agency's decision to close it. The hospital, opened in 1951, has 63 beds and serves more than 17,000 refugee families in the governorate, according to figures reported by WAFA. The demonstration brought together representatives of official institutions, the Popular Committee for Refugee Services and the local community.

Mohammad Khader, speaking for the governor of Qalqilya, called the hospital a vital health and humanitarian institution and said the responsibility for keeping it open could not be set aside for financial or administrative reasons. The protesters' demands were specific: reverse the closure, reopen the internal medicine and maternity departments, and protect the jobs and rights of the staff who work there.

The wards have been closing in stages. UNRWA shut the internal medicine department in December 2025 and the maternity department in March 2026 as part of cost-cutting measures, WAFA reported. Abdul Rahim Jabr, who heads the Popular Committee for Refugee Services, said health care is a right of refugees, not a favour, and that peaceful protests would continue until the demands are met.

The rally was the second in a fortnight. On 27 October the PLO's Refugee Affairs Department and camp committees held a demonstration in Balata refugee camp, in Nablus, against service cuts, staff dismissals and the Qalqilya plan. Nisreen Thawqan, the department's director for the northern West Bank, said then that donors would be asked to cover a shortfall of about $70 million in UNRWA's budget and to find a further $3 million to keep the hospital running.

UNRWA has not publicly detailed its plans for the site in the reports available, and the agency's acting leadership is under pressure from several directions. The PLO Executive Committee said on 25 October that it rejected any large-scale layoffs and urged the acting commissioner-general to tour donor capitals. On 6 November UN Secretary-General António Guterres reaffirmed his full support for the agency and called for its work to be fully funded.

Access to care across the West Bank is already strained. The World Health Organization counts 872 functioning health service points, of which 490 work only partially and 22 others are out of service, according to OCHA's latest report, and mobile clinics run by aid groups cover 227 locations that have no fixed facility. For refugees in Qalqilya, speakers at the protest said, the question is whether a hospital that has treated them for 75 years will still be there next year.

stories.title: Two Old City institutions shut in five days: a sports club closed and Burj al-Laqlaq sealed again
stories.short: Two Old City youth institutions closed in five days
stories.gist: Israeli police closed the Sons of Jerusalem Club on 5 November and renewed a six-month closure of the Burj al-Laqlaq society on 10 November.
body: Israeli authorities closed two Palestinian community institutions inside the walls of Jerusalem's Old City within five days this month. On Thursday 5 November the Sons of Jerusalem Club, in the Sa'diya neighbourhood, was shut under an order issued by National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, the Palestinian Authority's Jerusalem Governorate said. On Tuesday 10 November police raided the Burj al-Laqlaq Community Society and posted a notice closing it for six months, WAFA reported.

The Sons of Jerusalem Club is one of the Old City's long-established sports and social institutions, according to the governorate, and gives young residents a place to train, meet and organise activities. The governorate described the closure as part of a policy of restricting Palestinian national, sports and social bodies in the city. No public explanation of the order from the Israeli side was included in the reports available.

Burj al-Laqlaq takes its name from the Stork Tower at the north-eastern corner of the city wall. The society that operates there runs educational, sports and cultural programmes for children and teenagers, along with social activities and tutoring. According to the Wadi Hilweh Information Center, a local monitoring group, the new order covers all of the society's facilities with one exception: its kindergarten may stay open.

This is the second closure of the year for the society. Israeli forces first raided its premises on 17 February 2026 and ordered it shut for six months. It reopened on 13 August, which means it had been operating for less than three months when police returned on 10 November with a second six-month order. If the order runs its full term, the centre will be closed until May.

For young people in the Old City the two decisions remove much of the organised activity within walking distance. Athletes from Jerusalem clubs have been prominent in recent Palestinian sporting results: the delegation that won eight medals at a kickboxing World Cup in Tashkent in October included members of the Aswar Beit al-Maqdis Club and the Al-Bustan Silwan Association, WAFA reported at the time.

Israel has in the past closed Palestinian institutions in East Jerusalem on the grounds that they are linked to the Palestinian Authority, whose activity in the city it prohibits. Palestinians regard East Jerusalem as occupied territory and the closures as an attempt to hollow out communal life. The governorate said the latest measures narrow the spaces left to residents for sport, culture and social life.

stories.title: Why are 150,000 winter tents sitting outside Gaza while families sleep in flooded shelters?
stories.short: Why are 150,000 tents still waiting outside Gaza?
stories.gist: Aid agencies say entry restrictions, slow approvals and a $186.5 million funding gap keep shelter supplies outside while stocks inside run out.
body: The numbers do not add up for anyone standing in a flooded camp. According to OCHA, more than 150,000 tents bought by aid organisations and governments are stored outside Gaza and ready to move, including about 117,000 held by the Egyptian Relief Committee in Al-Arish, along with 300,000 tarpaulins and 500,000 blankets. Inside the Strip, the Shelter Cluster counted only about 2,800 tents and 76,000 tarpaulins in stock on 1 November, a week before the first storm arrived.

Need is on a different scale. The cluster estimates that Gaza requires about 121,000 tents, 561,000 tarpaulins, 57,000 emergency shelter kits and 1.7 million mattresses this winter. Not one emergency shelter kit is available, OCHA says, because the kits are built around timber and Israeli authorities continue to reject its entry. Only 4,993 mattresses were in stock. The Palestinian minister of social development, Samah Hamad, puts the requirement higher still, at about 200,000 tents and 200,000 tarpaulins.

Three obstacles recur in the UN reporting. The first is permission: OCHA says preparations were constrained by Israeli restrictions on supplies and equipment, and lists approvals for shelter items, engine oil, spare parts and heavy machinery as the most urgent need. Hamad told a press conference in Ramallah on 9 November that about 30 per cent of relief and shelter items allocated for the response were stranded at crossings, and that materials available this winter amount to a tenth of previous years' levels.

The second obstacle is money. The winter plan costs US$267.9 million and, even counting goods already on order, is short by US$186.5 million. The third is time. Agencies have about 59,000 tents and 703,000 tarpaulins under procurement, but OCHA warns that long lead times and approval delays mean much of this may not arrive until the second half of winter. Humanitarian cargo ready to ship has itself been shrinking because of funding constraints, the Logistics Cluster reports.

There is also a shortage of ground to pitch tents on. OCHA notes that Israeli restrictions on access to large parts of Gaza limit families' ability to move to safer areas, and Hamad said there is not enough suitable land to open new sites that meet minimum standards. About 950,000 people live in displacement sites at medium or high flood risk, according to a shelter assessment cited by the United Nations in its daily briefings in late October.

In the meantime the response is improvised. In the week to 2 November shelter partners reached 13,316 households with items including 791 tents, 5,496 winter clothing kits and 56,389 plastic sheets, and site teams have placed more than 135,000 sandbags since September. Aid groups say this buys days, not a season, and that the decisive step remains opening the crossings to the stock that has already been paid for.

stories.title: Five people, three of them children, die as rain-soaked sand cliff collapses on tents in Deir al-Balah
stories.short: Sand cliff collapse kills five in Deir al-Balah camp
stories.gist: A sand cliff loosened by rain fell on tents at a Deir al-Balah displacement site on 8 November, killing five people including three children.
body: A steep bank of sand collapsed onto tents sheltering displaced families in Deir al-Balah, in central Gaza, on the evening of Sunday 8 November, killing five people. WAFA, quoting rescue teams, said the first body recovered from under the sand was that of a woman, followed by four more victims, three of them children. The agency named the site as the Ard El-Rebat displacement camp and said five injured people were pulled out alive while the search went on.

Accounts of the toll differ slightly, as is common in the first hours after such an incident. OCHA, citing Civil Defense, located the collapse at Al Berka Reservoir west of Deir al-Balah and reported five dead, three children and two women, with one person injured. Speaking in New York on Monday, UN deputy spokesperson Farhan Haq referred to at least three children and one woman killed. Palestinian Social Development Minister Samah Hamad later gave five as the final figure.

The collapse came on the third day of the first major storm of the season. OCHA said the rain had already destroyed more than 6,000 family shelters across Gaza and that an infant had drowned at another displacement site. Because large parts of the Strip are off limits to Palestinians, the UN office noted, families have few options for moving voluntarily to safer and less flood-prone ground, and many remain camped on slopes, in low basins or beside damaged buildings.

At a joint press conference in Ramallah on 9 November, Hamad and the UN humanitarian coordinator Ramiz Alakbarov warned that winter threatens hundreds of thousands of displaced families. Hamad said about 2.1 million people in Gaza need winter protection, that more than 1,600 displacement sites face growing risks from pooling rainwater and broken sewers, and that roughly 4,000 buildings are at risk of collapse. She said at least 19 people, including children, died of hypothermia over the previous two winters.

Haq told reporters that Israeli restrictions were forcing aid workers to respond with what he called wholly inadequate equipment and shelter supplies. He relayed Alakbarov's appeal for the removal of unnecessary restrictions and delays on dewatering pumps, heavy machinery, tents, tarpaulins, blankets and winter clothing. Before the storm, a debris working group had reinforced about 130 vulnerable sites with more than 100,000 tons of rubble, according to OCHA, but hundreds of other sites had no such protection.

photo.caption: Archive: a displaced girl outside her family's tent in Deir al-Balah, August 2024.

stories.title: In Masafer Yatta, ten teachers held for five hours on the way home and a school raided a week later
stories.short: Masafer Yatta: teachers detained, school raided
stories.gist: The UN says ten Jinba school teachers were detained for about five hours on 1 November; a teacher was arrested at Al-Fakhit school on 8 November.
body: Israeli forces detained ten teachers from Jinba Basic School in Masafer Yatta, in the southern Hebron hills, for about five hours on 1 November as they were travelling home from work, OCHA reported. A week later, on Sunday 8 November, soldiers raided Al-Fakhit School in the same area and arrested a teacher, Mohammed Ahmed Hammad, who was taken to an unknown location, according to the local media activist Osama Makhamreh, quoted by WAFA.

Masafer Yatta is a cluster of small herding and farming hamlets that the Israeli army designates as Firing Zone 918, a live-fire training area. OCHA says movement restrictions there include the confiscation of vehicles and limits on coordinated access to the zone. For teachers and pupils alike, that turns the daily journey to and from school into the least predictable part of the day, and the detention on 1 November happened on exactly that journey.

The first week of November brought a series of incidents. On 5 November, Makhamreh told WAFA, soldiers raided homes and caves in Khirbet al-Tabban and two neighbouring hamlets and seized a car and tractors, one of them belonging to the Masafer Yatta council, that had been used to carry animal feed. On 9 November the army held exercises with tracked vehicles in Khirbet al-Fakhit, declared the area a closed military zone and kept residents out.

Water is a second pressure point. OCHA says emergency water trucking remains suspended in four Masafer Yatta communities, affecting 975 people, and that six other communities receive reduced deliveries because of movement restrictions and settler attacks. During the Hebron operation in late October the army also cut off villages near Masafer Yatta, and olive harvest access near settlements in the governorate was suspended.

The demolitions of recent months form the background. A chronology of the year compiled on Wikipedia from press reports records that Israel demolished the hamlet of Al-Tabban on 2 September, citing a Supreme Court ruling on Firing Zone 918, and carried out further demolitions in Jinba on 23 September. Residents and Israeli and international rights groups have argued for years that the firing-zone designation is being used to remove the communities.

Settler attacks add to the army's measures. On 10 November, WAFA reported, armed settlers drove a family out of its olive grove in Wadi Ma'in in Masafer Yatta and took the crop and equipment. Education partners working across the West Bank reached 2,840 pupils with emergency preparedness and explosive-hazard sessions in the last week of October, OCHA said. In Jinba and Al-Fakhit, the more immediate question is whether the teachers arrive.

photo.caption: Archive: the school in Al-Fakhit village, Masafer Yatta, 2025.

stories.title: First winter storm floods displacement sites across Gaza, damaging more than 23,000 family shelters
stories.short: First winter storm swamps Gaza's displacement sites
stories.gist: OCHA says rain from 6 November destroyed over 6,000 family shelters, damaged 17,400 more and left 3,900 households with none.
body: Heavy rain and strong winds that began on the evening of 6 November flooded displacement sites in all five governorates of the Gaza Strip, according to a situation report published by the UN humanitarian office OCHA. Preliminary figures gathered by the Site Management Cluster up to midnight on 7 November recorded about 268 weather alerts affecting more than 26,000 households. Over 6,000 family shelters were reported destroyed and 17,400 damaged, and more than 3,900 households were left with no shelter at all.

OCHA estimates that about 65 per cent of Gaza's population, roughly 1.4 million people, still live in tents or makeshift shelters. Civil Defense said water reached 1.5 metres in some places on 7 November. Its emergency rooms logged 2,166 distress calls in a single day, but rescue teams could physically reach only 218 of them; most callers were given advice over the phone. Gaza Municipality received another 251 incident reports and pointed to wrecked drainage networks and a lack of pumps and heavy machinery.

The official Palestinian news agency WAFA reported that rainwater poured into thousands of tents pitched on low ground and that two people were injured in northern Gaza when the wall of a building already damaged by bombardment gave way. The agency put the number of tents in use across the Strip at about 270,000, with more than 400,000 displaced people living in places exposed to flooding or close to the shoreline. Aid partners have identified at least 4,000 buildings at high risk of collapse.

Services were hit as well. OCHA said at least 55 learning spaces serving about 55,000 children were affected, and classes were suspended in 20 that were damaged. Eight community kitchens halved their output on 7 November, which meant about 25,000 fewer meals that day, before returning to normal on 8 November. Water entered departments at Nasser Medical Complex, the basement of the Patient's Friends Benevolent Society Hospital was flooded, and several partners suspended mobile clinics for a day or more.

Relief teams installed 50,000 sandbags over two days, distributed winter clothes to 3,364 households in Khan Younis and Deir al-Balah, and operated 15 dewatering pumps. By 8 November heavy machinery was supporting 200 affected sites. OCHA nonetheless described partners as overwhelmed by appeals. It said stocks of tents, tarpaulins and blankets inside Gaza are nearly exhausted, while more than 150,000 tents, 300,000 tarpaulins and 500,000 blankets are waiting outside the territory.

The report lists three urgent needs: Israeli approval to bring in shelter items, engine oil, spare parts and heavy machinery; vacuum trucks, mobile pumps and hoses; and more humanitarian funding. Mine action teams added a separate warning that floodwater can uncover unexploded ordnance or carry it into areas previously considered clear. OCHA stressed that all its figures are preliminary and subject to verification as assessments continue across the affected sites.

stories.title: From Stockholm's Odenplan to the Port of Elizabeth: five solidarity actions of the past three weeks
stories.short: Five solidarity actions, from Stockholm to New Jersey
stories.gist: Marches in Stockholm, Chicago, Berlin and Hanover, a port protest in New Jersey and a cross-country US convoy all called for an end to arms flows.
body: Stockholm, 7 November. Hundreds of people gathered at Odenplan square on Saturday evening after a call from several civil society organisations, WAFA reported. They protested against Israeli attacks on Gaza, the West Bank and Lebanon and against violations of the ceasefire. Placards referred to children killed in Gaza, to schools and hospitals, and to food shortages. The demonstrators asked the Swedish government to suspend arms sales to Israel.

Chicago, reported 9 November. A march through the city brought together activists calling for an end to the war in Gaza and to US support for Israel, according to the agency's report, which did not give the exact date or a crowd estimate. Marchers carried Palestinian flags. The demonstration also took up the rights of immigrants in the United States, and speakers stressed the importance of sustained local organising to put pressure on the administration in Washington.

Berlin and Hanover, 25 October. Demonstrations were held in several German cities on the Sunday after Israel sealed the West Bank. Hundreds marched in Hanover with Palestinian flags and watermelon symbols, and hundreds more in Berlin, where speakers condemned what they called starvation policies in Gaza and the escalating violence in the West Bank. Participants called for an immediate end to the war and for the protection of civilians.

Port of Elizabeth, New Jersey, 1 November. Activists drove in procession through the port area to oppose the export and transfer of weapons to Israel and called for a boycott of the Israeli shipping line Zim. Organisers said the action was one of a series held that week at more than 100 ports in at least 22 countries, involving port workers and trade unions as well as campaigners. Those figures are the organisers' own.

Los Angeles to Washington, 17 to 26 October. A convoy of 42 people calling itself the 2026 Freedom Convoy USA set out from the Israeli consulate in Los Angeles on a ten-day drive across the country. Its route ran through Las Vegas, Albuquerque, Tulsa, St Louis and Chicago, among other stops. It planned to deliver a petition titled 'We the People' to congressional offices ahead of the 3 November midterm elections.

The convoy's participants included members of religious groups, former government employees and military veterans, WAFA reported. Their argument was framed around domestic priorities: money spent on military support for Israel, they said, should go to health care, housing, education and childcare. On election day itself President Donald Trump said in a television interview that annual US funding to Israel, about $3.8 billion, would end this year under an agreement with Benjamin Netanyahu.

The common thread in all five is arms. Whether in a Swedish square, an American port or a convoy crossing the Midwest, the demand addressed to governments was the same: stop supplying weapons. The crowds described in the reports were in the hundreds in Stockholm, Berlin and Hanover, far smaller than the mass marches of 2023 and 2024, but the actions were spread across at least three countries in three weeks.

stories.title: The olive harvest in numbers: 377 settler attacks since September, more than any season on UN record
stories.short: Olive harvest in numbers: a record 377 settler attacks
stories.gist: OCHA counted 377 harvest-related settler attacks between 1 September and 2 November, more than in any previous olive season it has recorded.
body: 377. That is the number of olive-harvest-related attacks by Israeli settlers that the UN humanitarian office OCHA recorded across the West Bank between 1 September and 2 November, each one causing casualties, property damage or both. It is higher than the total for any previous harvest season in the office's records. For comparison, a group of UN experts said on 19 October that 178 such attacks were documented during the whole of the 2025 harvest, affecting 88 towns and villages.

457. OCHA logged that many settler attacks of all kinds in October up to the 31st, the highest monthly figure since the UN began documenting such incidents in 2006. In the week of 27 October to 2 November alone there were 64 attacks in 48 communities, against a weekly average of 53 for 2026. Fifty-eight Palestinians were injured that week, 43 of them by settlers and 15 by Israeli forces, and 44 of the injuries were linked to the harvest.

674. The Palestinian Authority's Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission uses a wider definition that also counts actions by soldiers. It documented 674 attacks on farmers and olive trees between 1 October and 6 November, 520 by settlers and 154 by Israeli forces. Nablus governorate recorded 230, Ramallah and al-Bireh 130 and Salfit 129, together almost three quarters of the total. The commission counted 407 attacks in the 2024 season and 333 in 2023.

2,974. That is the commission's estimate of olive trees damaged so far, and it says figures were unavailable for some incidents. It also lists 91 cases of olives being stolen, 37 thefts or confiscations of equipment, 76 physical assaults and 249 incidents of intimidation. One Palestinian died of wounds from settler gunfire sustained while harvesting, the commission said. Its figures are its own and are not directly comparable with OCHA's.

15. In Deir Ammar, west of Ramallah, access to groves near a settlement was limited to three days and to 15 farmers aged over 40, OCHA reported; an 82-year-old farmer there was assaulted. In Beit Iksa, near Jerusalem, farmers were forced out of their groves despite prior coordination with the army, and settlers reportedly picked about 30 trees. Eight of the week's 41 harvest incidents took place in Areas A and B, which are under Palestinian civil administration.

42. That is the age of Samar Zidan, who was picking olives with her husband and children west of Deir Istiya, in Salfit governorate, on 11 November when she was hit in the head by a stone thrown by settlers, according to local sources quoted by WAFA. Her injury was described as moderate. Residents say attacks in the area have increased since a herding outpost was set up nearby.

80 per cent. Aid groups have supplied harvesting tools and machinery in nearly 80 per cent of identified hotspots, OCHA says, and volunteers provide a protective presence in the groves. But the office concedes that in most places help reaches only a limited number of pickers, because of funding shortfalls, violence and Israeli restrictions. The UN experts warned that destroying a mature olive tree costs a family far more than one season's crop.

stories.title: What is UNRWA, and why are refugees in the West Bank protesting against cuts to its services?
stories.short: What is UNRWA, and why is it cutting services?
stories.gist: The UN agency for Palestine refugees faces a shortfall of about $70 million and is weighing layoffs and the closure of its Qalqilya hospital.
body: UNRWA is the United Nations Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East. The General Assembly created it by Resolution 302 after the 1948 war to assist Palestinians who had lost their homes, and its mandate has been renewed ever since in the absence of a political settlement. It runs schools, clinics and relief programmes for registered refugees in Gaza, the West Bank including East Jerusalem, Jordan, Lebanon and Syria.

Unlike most UN bodies, UNRWA delivers services directly, and almost all of its staff are Palestinian teachers, doctors, nurses and sanitation workers. It depends on voluntary contributions from governments. That combination makes it sensitive to any drop in funding: when donors hold back, the effect is felt within weeks in classrooms and health centres, and in the salaries of its own employees.

That is the situation now. The PLO Executive Committee said on 25 October that about $70 million is needed urgently to meet immediate needs and pay staff salaries for November and December. It said the agency's management was considering large-scale layoffs, which it rejected, arguing that staff are the backbone of the agency and that dismissing them would not solve the crisis. It urged the acting commissioner-general to tour donor capitals.

The cuts are already visible in the West Bank. UNRWA closed the internal medicine ward of its hospital in Qalqilya in December 2025 and the maternity ward in March 2026, and has decided to close the 63-bed hospital altogether, according to WAFA. Refugee committees protested in Balata camp, in Nablus, on 27 October and in the hospital courtyard on 10 November. A PLO official put the cost of keeping the hospital open at an additional $3 million.

The agency is under pressure on other fronts too. In Gaza, OCHA reported in late 2025 that Israeli authorities were barring UNRWA from bringing aid in directly, even as its schools sheltered tens of thousands of displaced people. In the northern West Bank, tens of thousands of refugees remain displaced from the Jenin, Tulkarm and Nur Shams camps after Israeli military operations that began in early 2025; a UN inquiry put the figure at 34,176 in August.

Diplomatic support has not translated into money. UNESCO's executive board unanimously adopted a resolution in October supporting the continuity of UNRWA's education work, and on 6 November the UN secretary-general, António Guterres, reaffirmed his full commitment to defending the agency and called for it to be fully funded. The PLO has proposed a joint committee with the host countries to lead a funding campaign. Until donors respond, the choice in front of the agency is which services to stop.

photo.caption: Archive: a street in Balata refugee camp, Nablus, April 2011.

stories.title: Israel orders deportation of 12 foreign volunteers detained while helping with olive harvest near Ramallah
stories.short: Israel to deport 12 olive-harvest volunteers
stories.gist: Seventeen people were detained in Kafr Ni'ma on 6 November; five Germans, four Italians, two Canadians and an American were ordered deported.
body: Israeli authorities decided to deport 12 international volunteers who were detained on Friday 6 November while helping Palestinian farmers pick olives in the village of Kafr Ni'ma, west of Ramallah, according to the Faza'a campaign, which organises volunteers for the harvest. The group said a lawyer following the case had been told the activists would be removed on Saturday morning. They are five Germans, four Italians, two Canadians and one American.

Seventeen people were detained in all. Besides the 12 volunteers there were two foreign journalists and three Palestinians, one of them a woman. Faza'a said the three Palestinians were its Ramallah coordinator and two farmers, and that soldiers assaulted the farmers before taking them away. The detainees were first taken to a nearby military post, the campaign said in its statement.

The campaign's account, carried by WAFA, is that a group of settlers attacked the pickers near Jabal al-Risan, on the edge of the village, and held them by force, and that the army then detained those who had been attacked. There was no account of the incident from the Israeli military in the reports available. The same day, soldiers expelled foreign activists and journalists from a village north-east of Ramallah, the agency reported.

It was not the first such case this season. Faza'a said several foreign activists were detained in Masafer Yatta, south of Hebron, on 22 October and later deported. Israel's settler leadership said in early October that the defence minister, Israel Katz, had ordered a ban on pro-Palestinian activists assisting olive harvesters in the West Bank, according to a chronology of the year's events.

Faza'a condemned the deportations as an attempt to silence witnesses to settler attacks, to prevent violations from being documented and to obstruct international efforts to help farmers reach their land. It said it would continue its activities across the West Bank with Palestinian and international volunteers for the rest of the season, to support farmers and strengthen their presence on their land.

The UN describes the presence of volunteers as one of the few protective measures available. OCHA said this month that protection partners were supporting volunteer harvest campaigns and providing a protective presence, but that help reaches only a limited number of pickers. Volunteers have themselves been hurt: two Israeli solidarity activists were injured by settlers near Aqraba on 1 November, and a protective-presence volunteer was injured in Kafr Malik, the office reported.

photo.caption: Archive: the village of Kafr Ni'ma, west of Ramallah, seen from the east in February 2019.

stories.title: Why are doctors in Gaza asking for an independent inquiry into a rise in birth defects?
stories.short: Why do Gaza doctors want a birth-defects inquiry?
stories.gist: Gaza recorded 260 congenital anomalies in nine months of 2026 against 184 in all of 2022, and doctors say the cause has not been established.
body: A medical source in Gaza told WAFA on 6 November that 260 cases of congenital anomalies were recorded among newborns in the first nine months of 2026. That is already more than the 184 cases reported in the whole of 2022, the last full year before the war. The same source said 322 cases were recorded in 2025, an increase of 75 per cent on 2022, and asked that the trend be examined by outside specialists.

The source was careful about what the figures do and do not show. Raw case counts, the report notes, do not establish the rate of anomalies among all births and do not identify a cause. That caution is the reason for the request: the source called for an independent international scientific investigation, something beyond the capacity of a health system that, by the Red Crescent's account this week, currently struggles to run even basic laboratory tests.

Three possible factors were named for investigators to examine: malnutrition among mothers, exposure to environmental pollutants, and the disruption of antenatal care during the war. The conditions being recorded include cleft lip and palate, shortened upper limbs, umbilical hernias and ambiguous external genitalia that make it hard to determine a baby's sex at birth. One child may have more than one anomaly, the source said, so the number of affected babies may be lower than the case count.

Other data point to the strain on mothers and babies. OCHA's report of 5 November, citing the Health Cluster, says neonatal units in Gaza ran at 151 per cent occupancy in September and special care baby units at 199 per cent, and that nearly 63 per cent of deliveries were classed as high-risk. The cluster estimates that between 123 and 179 additional neonatal beds are needed in the last quarter of the year.

The environmental question is also open. In a statement on 6 November the Palestinian Environmental Quality Authority estimated that Gaza holds between 61 and 68 million tons of rubble, about four million tons of hazardous waste and at least 50,000 tons of asbestos, and that around 120,000 cubic metres of untreated wastewater is released every day. The authority's figures are its own estimates and have not been independently verified.

WAFA's report recalls that Human Rights Watch documented serious risks to pregnant women in Gaza in a report published on 28 January 2025, pointing to the blockade, the destruction of health facilities and shortages of food, water and medicine. Aid partners say they have bought postpartum kits and warming items for newborns this winter. Whether the rise in recorded anomalies reflects real change, better reporting or both is exactly what the doctors want an outside inquiry to settle.

stories.title: Six demolitions in two weeks: the East Jerusalem families who lost homes, some by their own hands
stories.short: Six Jerusalem demolitions in a fortnight, case by case
stories.gist: Between 25 October and 6 November at least six demolition cases were reported in and around East Jerusalem, four carried out by the owners.
body: Beit Hanina, 25 October. Fawaz al-Rajabi demolished his own 60-square-metre house after receiving a written order, the Wadi Hilweh Information Center reported. The house was built 15 years ago and was home to al-Rajabi, his wife and their five children. He had already paid fines totalling 60,000 shekels for building without a permit. Owners who decline to demolish are billed for the municipality's bulldozers.

Silwan, 28 October. Musa al-Awar was made to pull down his house in the Ein al-Lawza area, south of the Old City, according to the Palestinian Authority's Jerusalem Governorate. Beit Hanina, 31 October. Jihad Mutawir demolished a building of two apartments, his own and his son's, in the al-Marwaha neighbourhood; the governorate said more than seven people were left without a home. In both cases the stated reason was the lack of a building permit.

Silwan, 4 November. Municipal bulldozers demolished the home of Suleiman Abu Subaih in the al-Bustan neighbourhood. The governorate said the 80-square-metre house was 25 years old, that Abu Subaih has particular health needs after the amputation of a leg, and that crews damaged roads and uprooted trees in the neighbourhood to clear a route to the building. He lived there with his wife.

Jerusalem governorate, 5 November. Bulldozers demolished several homes and a residential building in a town that WAFA's report did not name, after residents were made to empty them. The governorate listed five owners, Ziad al-Sheikh, Ghazi al-Sheikh, Wael Samara, Murad Shammasneh and Ahmad al-Dali, and said 20 people were displaced. The same day, the Palestinian foreign ministry said about half the structures of the Bedouin community of Bir al-Maskub, east of the city, were destroyed.

Jabal al-Mukabber, 6 November. Two relatives, Mar'i Jamil Ja'abees and Mohammed Aziz Ja'abees, demolished their own houses in the al-Sal'a area on a Friday morning. Each house measured about 50 square metres and was built in 2020; together they housed 18 people. The families had earlier paid 25,000 shekels in an attempt to prevent the demolitions, local sources told WAFA.

The cases follow a pattern the UN has documented for years. OCHA recorded 31 Palestinian-owned structures demolished or self-demolished across the West Bank, including East Jerusalem, between 27 October and 2 November, displacing 71 people of whom 38 were children; 24 were destroyed for lack of an Israeli-issued permit. The UN office has described such permits as almost impossible for Palestinians to obtain. Israel says it is enforcing planning law.

photo.caption: Archive: the Jabal al-Mukabber neighbourhood of East Jerusalem, March 2022.

stories.title: How does aid reach Gaza now, and why did the number of trucks fall by more than a quarter in a week?
stories.short: How does aid get into Gaza now?
stories.gist: Most cargo is offloaded at Kerem Shalom; the UN manifested 466 trucks in the last week of October, 28 per cent fewer than the week before.
body: Almost everything that reaches Gaza's warehouses passes through one point. In its report for 27 October to 2 November, OCHA says the Logistics Cluster manifested 466 UN and partner trucks for entry between 26 October and 1 November, and 397 of them were offloaded on the Israeli side of the Kerem Shalom crossing. That cargo had started its journey in three places: 195 truckloads came from the port of Ashdod, 127 from Egypt and 28 from Jordan.

The total was 28 per cent lower than the previous week. Part of the explanation is financial. Partners told OCHA that the amount of humanitarian cargo available to ship is declining because of funding constraints, and the World Food Programme announced on 19 October that it would cut assistance to about 500,000 people. Part is political: the UN said transport was suspended on 27 October because Israel closed Kerem Shalom for its election day.

Commercial goods use the same gate. Private trucks resumed through Kerem Shalom after a suspension in mid-October, which OCHA says brought the prices of basic commodities back to their early-October levels. Data from the Gaza Chamber of Commerce show 498 commercial truckloads entering between 26 October and 1 November. During the suspension, the head of Gaza's bakers' association told WAFA on 22 October that flour stocks were exhausted and only seven of 20 commercial bakeries were still working.

The route from Egypt is now in doubt. On the evening of 1 November, OCHA reports, Israeli authorities notified UN agencies that humanitarian and commercial shipments from Egypt would be suspended, with some exceptions, citing concerns about smuggling. The Food Security Sector warned that if the suspension lasts, daily cooked meals could fall from about 600,000 to 330,000, a cut of roughly 45 per cent, and bread production from 160 to 139 metric tons a day.

Entry is only half the journey. Trucks inside Gaza depend on engine oil, lubricants and spare parts that Israel tightly restricts, and OCHA says only half of the waste-collection fleet is still running. One aid partner could not deliver 7,250 planned meals on 7 November because its vehicles lacked oil and parts and roads were flooded. On 3 November small-arms fire was reported close to a UN-organised convoy in Rafah and near a UN-contracted facility in Deir al-Balah.

People cross in far smaller numbers than goods. OCHA recorded 107 patients, 38 of them children, leaving with 119 companions through Rafah and Kerem Shalom for Egypt and Jordan in the week to 2 November. On 9 November, WAFA reported, 23 patients and 28 companions departed through Rafah, and four people were turned back. For now, 21 subsidised bakeries and 90 community kitchens remain the daily measure of what gets in.

stories.title: Seven figures from the Palestinian environment authority's count of 760 violations in the West Bank
stories.short: 760 environmental violations logged in West Bank this year
stories.gist: The Environmental Quality Authority says it logged 760 environmental violations by Israeli forces and settlers from January to September 2026.
body: The Palestinian Environmental Quality Authority marked the UN's day for preventing the exploitation of the environment in war, 6 November, by publishing its tally for the first nine months of 2026: 760 environmental violations in the West Bank that it attributes to Israeli forces and settlers. The figures are the authority's own and were reported by WAFA. Seven of them give a sense of what is being counted, and of how broadly the authority defines environmental harm.

203 and 178. The largest category, 203 incidents, concerns farmland and nature reserves: olive groves bulldozed, settlement roads cut through fields, thousands of dunums seized, land fenced off for herding outposts and greenhouses burned. A further 178 incidents targeted forests and vegetation. The authority says thousands of fruit-bearing and perennial trees were uprooted, about 100,000 of them olive trees by the end of September, and that wheat and barley fields were set alight.

$67 million. That is the authority's estimate of losses from the destruction of trees and vegetation alone. The UN's own count for the current olive season is narrower but points the same way: OCHA recorded 377 harvest-related settler attacks between 1 September and 2 November, more than in any previous season, and UN experts said more than 6,000 trees and saplings were vandalised during the 2025 harvest.

185. The authority logged this many violations involving hazardous waste and demolition debris, thousands of tons of construction rubble concentrated in Jenin and Tulkarm governorates and their refugee camps, where Israeli military operations since early 2025 have demolished large numbers of buildings. Five more incidents damaged sewage networks in the two camps and halted wastewater drainage for residents, it said.

37 and 35. Water was the target in 72 incidents: 37 against sources, including wells that were filled in or buried, springs destroyed or taken over and tanks wrecked, and 35 against pipelines and irrigation networks. The authority says the main pipe serving the Birin area was destroyed at Khallet al-Furn, cutting off about 450 people, and that a pipe to Ad-Duqaiqa village in Hebron governorate was severed, leaving 700 residents without water.

52. This is the number of attacks on livestock and food security, including the theft of hundreds of animals and the release of settlers' herds onto cultivated land. The practice has continued into the autumn: on 9 November, WAFA reported, settlers let livestock loose on Palestinian farmland in Hebron governorate, damaging crops, and on 4 November the agency reported the theft of a banana harvest from Palestinian land in Nablus governorate.

The authority argues that the pattern amounts to environmental war crimes under the Rome Statute and the Geneva Conventions, a legal assessment that is its own. Its statement also covered Gaza, where it estimates that 82 per cent of farmland and 97 per cent of fruit and olive trees have been destroyed or bulldozed. The seven categories it itemised add up to 695, so about 65 of the 760 incidents are not broken down in the published summary.

stories.title: What is the E1 plan, and why did a Bedouin hamlet's demolition raise alarm that it has begun?
stories.short: What is the E1 plan east of Jerusalem?
stories.gist: E1 is a planned settlement of 3,401 homes between Jerusalem and Ma'ale Adumim; Palestinians say demolitions at Bir al-Maskub mark its start.
body: E1 is the name of a tract of hills between East Jerusalem and the large settlement of Ma'ale Adumim. Israel has had plans to build there for decades and repeatedly shelved them under international pressure, because construction would close the last open corridor linking the northern and southern West Bank past Jerusalem. Two tenders are now on the books for a total of 3,401 housing units, according to the Palestinian Authority's Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission.

The larger tender, No. 460/2025, covers 2,167 units; a second, No. 186/2026, covers 1,234. On 5 November the timetable for the first was revised: publication of the tender documents and the opening of bidding moved from 25 October to 1 December, and the closing date from 21 to 28 December. The commission stressed that this is a change of schedule only, not a cancellation or a reduction in the number of homes.

On the same day the Palestinian foreign ministry said Israeli forces had demolished about half of the structures of Bir al-Maskub, a Bedouin community inside the planning area, including four residential clusters, and handed out demolition notices for everything that remained. The ministry called it a shift from planning and paperwork to implementation on the ground, and warned that other Bedouin communities in the area could be next.

The ministry's argument is that E1 would cut the West Bank in two, separate East Jerusalem from its Palestinian surroundings and so make a contiguous Palestinian state impossible. It accused Israel's caretaker government of using the transition after the 27 October election to create facts on the ground. It called on other governments, and on the United States in particular, to act to stop the demolitions before they spread to neighbouring communities.

Foreign governments have gone beyond statements. Britain's foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said on 18 October that the tender was a direct threat to a two-state solution and addressed companies directly: the UK, he said, has created powers to sanction individuals and firms involved in building settlements such as E1, and bidders should expect legal and reputational consequences. He also repeated a commitment to legislate against imports of settlement goods.

Bir al-Maskub is one of several herding communities around the Jerusalem to Jericho road, of which Khan al-Ahmar is the best known. On 8 November settlers from a nearby outpost stoned homes in another Bedouin community close to Khan al-Ahmar before residents drove them off, the Jerusalem Governorate said. Israel maintains that the communities were built without permits on state land; residents say they have nowhere else to go.

photo.caption: Archive: Khan al-Ahmar, a Bedouin community in the same area east of Jerusalem, January 2025. Bir al-Maskub itself is not pictured.

stories.title: Why has the UK Supreme Court been asked to rule on the ban on the protest group Palestine Action?
stories.short: Why is the UK's top court reviewing the Palestine Action ban?
stories.gist: The court heard an appeal on 4-5 November on whether the 2025 ban breaches free expression and assembly rights; judgment is still pending.
body: Britain's Supreme Court spent 4 and 5 November hearing the final domestic appeal against the government's decision to ban Palestine Action under terrorism law. The appeal was brought by Huda Ammori, a co-founder of the direct-action group. The justices have reserved judgment, which is expected in December or January. Their ruling will settle a legal fight that has run for sixteen months and produced two contradictory decisions from the courts below.

The ban dates from July 2025. The House of Commons voted 385 to 26 on 2 July to proscribe the group, in an order that also listed two neo-Nazi organisations, and the measure took effect on 5 July under the Terrorism Act 2000. From that date, membership of the group or public expressions of support for it became criminal offences. Ammori went to the High Court the day before the ban took effect.

She won there. On 13 February 2026 three High Court judges ruled unanimously that the proscription was unlawful, both because it breached rights protected by the Human Rights Act and because the home secretary had not applied her own policy. Amnesty International and Liberty had intervened in the case, and the UN special rapporteur on counter-terrorism made submissions. The court delayed quashing the order so the government could appeal.

The government won the next round. On 15 June a five-judge Court of Appeal overturned the High Court; the lady chief justice, Baroness Carr, called the ban a justified and proportionate interference with individual rights. On 29 July the Supreme Court agreed to hear a further appeal, limited to one question: whether proscription is compatible with Articles 10 and 11 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protect freedom of expression and of assembly.

The stakes are measured in arrests. At least 3,070 people were arrested between the ban and the end of April 2026, most for holding signs expressing support for the group at silent sit-ins in Parliament Square and Trafalgar Square, according to figures collected on the group's Wikipedia page, and more than 600 others in a later wave. The Metropolitan Police spent £8.73 million policing four days of such protests.

If Ammori succeeds, the proscription falls and the basis for the arrests made under it is called into question; if she fails, she has said she will take the case to the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg. Either way the judgment will define how far a British government can go in using counter-terrorism powers against a protest movement, a question that reaches well beyond campaigning on Palestine.

stories.title: Israeli courts reject two petitions seeking the release of 14 Gaza doctors held without charge
stories.short: Courts refuse to free 14 detained Gaza doctors
stories.gist: Physicians for Human Rights-Israel says the 14 doctors, some held for more than two years, include hospital directors and specialists.
body: Israeli courts have rejected two petitions filed by the rights group Physicians for Human Rights-Israel for the release of 14 Palestinian doctors from Gaza, WAFA reported in a dispatch dated 5 November. The organisation says the doctors are being held in Israeli prisons without charge or trial, and that some of them have been in detention for more than two years. The report does not name the doctors or give details of the judges' reasoning.

Naji Abbas of Physicians for Human Rights-Israel said the group includes hospital directors and specialists in critical fields of medicine. In his view the two rulings show the scale of the violations against detained medical staff and the failure of the Israeli judiciary to protect their rights. Detainees, he argued, should not lose their medical rights because of their public profile or because of security allegations made against them.

Abbas framed the case as a matter of patient care as well as individual liberty. Israel cannot continue to hold doctors without trial, he said, because it deprives patients in Gaza of their care while denying the doctors themselves basic medical treatment. The organisation's petitions asked for the doctors to be released; it was not clear from the report whether it intends to take the cases further or to file new applications.

The staffing gap is acknowledged across the health sector. When Japan and the World Health Organization signed a $1.97 million grant on 10 November, the announcement said Gaza's health system faces immense pressure from shortages of health personnel, growing patient needs and rising demand for specialised services. Part of the money will train 100 local emergency medical team members so that Gaza relies less on visiting foreign teams.

Detention conditions are a concern in their own right. The Palestinian Prisoners' Society said on 8 November that testimony gathered by its lawyers in October and early November indicated about 80 per cent of detainees had scabies, which it linked to a severe shortage of clothing and a lack of treatment. Palestinian detainee bodies put the number of people held in Israeli prisons at more than 9,300, including about 90 women.

Israel says it detains people from Gaza on security grounds; the petitions concerned doctors against whom, according to the rights group, no charges have been brought. A WAFA feature published on 1 November described a similar pattern in the West Bank, profiling a 71-year-old general practitioner, Mazen al-Rantisi, who was held for four months and who said nine other doctors were detained in the same period.

stories.title: African Union, OIC and Arab League jointly call for Israeli withdrawal and second phase of Gaza ceasefire
stories.short: AU, OIC and Arab League issue joint call on Palestine
stories.gist: Meeting in Addis Ababa, the three organisations called for an end to the occupation, a Palestinian state and reopening of all Gaza crossings.
body: The African Union Commission, the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation and the League of Arab States issued a joint statement on Thursday 5 November calling for an end to Israel's occupation of Palestinian territory and an immediate and unconditional withdrawal. The statement followed a consultative meeting held the previous day at the African Union's headquarters in Addis Ababa, part of a three-way coordination mechanism the organisations have set up on Palestine.

Between them the three bodies count most of the states of Africa, the Arab world and the wider Muslim world among their members. Their statement backs an independent, sovereign Palestinian state on the lines of 4 June 1967 with East Jerusalem as its capital, in accordance with UN resolutions and the Arab Peace Initiative, and commits them to practical steps towards a two-state solution, including follow-up to the 2025 New York Declaration.

On Gaza, the organisations called for the second phase of the ceasefire agreement to be implemented in a way that leads to a permanent end to hostilities, the lifting of the blockade and the reopening of all crossings for the safe and unhindered delivery of aid. They said reconstruction must begin, and rejected any plan to displace Palestinians from Gaza or the West Bank, which they described as a war crime.

The statement devotes several paragraphs to the West Bank. It reaffirms that all Israeli settlements in occupied territory are illegal and calls for them to be dismantled, warns of escalating violence by extremist settlers acting under army protection, and calls for settlers to be disarmed in line with Security Council Resolution 904 of 1994. It welcomes the UN Human Rights Council's database of companies doing business in settlements.

On Jerusalem, the three organisations urged countries that have moved their embassies to the city, or announced plans to, to reverse those decisions. They called for the preservation of the historical and legal status quo at Islamic and Christian holy sites, Al-Aqsa Mosque in particular. They also condemned the ill-treatment of Palestinian prisoners and asked Israel to disclose the whereabouts of detainees.

The Palestinian Authority welcomed the statement. The text describes the Palestine Liberation Organization as the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people, calls for support to the Palestinian government so that it can assume its responsibilities in all of the occupied territory including Gaza, and demands that Israel release withheld Palestinian tax revenues in full. It also urges that Israeli forces be held to account before national and international courts.

stories.title: 'For the first time I have my own chair': three Gaza siblings born without legs receive custom aids
stories.short: Three Gaza siblings get wheelchairs built for them
stories.gist: Anas, Mohammad and Sujood Al-Sharif received wheelchairs, writing aids and walking supports made in Gaza by the NGO EducAid with UN funding.
body: Sujood Al-Sharif is 17 and until recently had never had a wheelchair that was hers. She and her brothers Mohammad, 15, and Anas, 10, were all born without legs and with two fingers on each hand. A story published by the UN humanitarian office OCHA on 5 November describes how the three received equipment designed around their bodies and their school day, paid for by the occupied Palestinian territory Humanitarian Fund and delivered by the international organisation EducAid.

For Sujood the package included a size-40 wheelchair with a detachable dining table, an adjustable slanted writing table, a waterproof shield for the lower body and hand supports for walking. She told the team that she sleeps in the chair so that her siblings cannot take it, and that it made her feel somebody cares about her. Writing used to exhaust her because she had to lie down to do it. She says she wants to study media.

Anas, the youngest, had his existing wheelchair serviced and upgraded, and was given a customised pen grip. Before, the pen kept slipping out of his hand, he moved mostly by crawling on his hands, and his mother often had to carry him. His mother told OCHA the difference was huge, particularly for writing and eating. EducAid began supporting him in 2025, while the war was still under way, according to the account.

Mohammad's aids were built after staff assessed what he needed both at school and at home. EducAid's own workshops produced the devices, among them a small skateboard-style seat that he enjoys using to get around, hand grips that his mother says protect him from wounds and slipping, and a commode chair that she said changed daily life. Mohammad's own verdict was practical: with the table and the shield, his clothes no longer get dirty.

A teacher quoted in the story said the three stand out in class, are eager to learn and had started to write more effectively. The article does not say where in Gaza the family lives; Sujood mentions leaving her tent, which suggests they are among the displaced. A separate OCHA report on the 6 to 8 November storm found that flooding hit two sites for people with disabilities, affecting 200 families, and described such households as facing heightened risk.

The Humanitarian Fund is a pooled fund managed by OCHA that channels donor money to aid organisations working in Gaza and the West Bank. The UN's news service carried the siblings' story on 7 November. Aid agencies estimate that thousands of children in Gaza now live with life-changing injuries, on top of those, like the Al-Sharif children, whose disabilities date from birth and whose equipment was lost, worn out or never available.

stories.title: Israel declares 2,536 dunums belonging to three villages north-west of Ramallah 'state property'
stories.short: 2,536 dunums near Ramallah declared 'state property'
stories.gist: A 3 November declaration covers land of Beitillu, al-Mazra'a al-Qibliya and Deir Ammar; owners have 45 days to object.
body: Israeli authorities have declared 2,536.44 dunums of land belonging to the villages of Beitillu, al-Mazra'a al-Qibliya and Deir Ammar, north-west of Ramallah, to be state property, the Palestinian Authority's Wall and Settlement Resistance Commission said on 4 November. The declaration was issued a day earlier and rests on Military Order No. 59 of 1967 concerning government property, according to the commission's statement carried by WAFA. A dunum is 1,000 square metres.

The land lies around the settlement of Kerem Reim. The commission said the declared area is spread over several registered land blocks in the three villages and that the accompanying map shows large, irregular shapes with excluded parcels scattered inside them. That makes it necessary, it said, to check each affected plot against the declared boundary and against ownership documents before owners can know exactly what they stand to lose.

In the commission's analysis, the measure would make it easier to join up the settlements of the Talmonim bloc, in particular Kerem Reim, Neria and Nahliel, and to extend them towards Talmon and Dolev. It said herding outposts already project control beyond the built-up areas by chasing farmers and shepherds off land between settlement sites, and warned that the cumulative effect is to break up the Palestinian countryside from Halamish and Ateret down to Dolev.

Anyone claiming rights to the land may object within 45 days of the declaration being posted on the land itself and at liaison offices. Objections go to a committee at the Ofer military camp. The commission urged landowners, village councils and legal organisations to collect title deeds, records of cultivation and land use, and documentation of occasions when farmers were attacked or kept off their plots, and to file quickly.

The declaration is one of several land measures reported in the same fortnight. The commission said Israel issued tenders on 3 and 5 November for 91 housing units in the settlement of Oranit, on land of Qalqilya governorate, and a tender on 9 November for 732 units in Gva'ot, west of Bethlehem. Earlier, on 19 October, WAFA reported a separate declaration covering 182.81 dunums in Bethlehem and Hebron governorates.

Israel regards land it declares state property as available for allocation by its custodian of government property; Palestinians and most of the international community consider settlements in occupied territory illegal under international law. UN experts noted in October that the army has changed its policy this year so that Palestinians can no longer obtain permits to harvest olives on plots Israel classifies as state land, even where families have picked them for generations.

photo.caption: Archive: the village of Beitillu, north-west of Ramallah, photographed from a nearby hilltop in April 2026.

stories.title: A 12-year-old who drove a cart to feed his family is back in class in Deir al-Balah, with help
stories.short: From cart driver back to pupil at 12
stories.gist: A boy who lost his mother in a 2024 strike and left learning to work has returned to school after counselling and family support, OCHA reports.
body: The boy in the story is called Shadi, which is not his real name. He is 12 and comes from Deir al-Balah. In January 2024 an Israeli air strike hit his home, killing his mother, his grandmother, his aunts and other relatives and critically injuring his father, according to an account published by the UN humanitarian office OCHA on 4 November. Shadi was hurt too, and his injuries affected both his eyesight and his speech.

The family ended up at a displacement site in the same town. Relatives noticed that the boy had become quiet, withdrawn and fearful. He stopped going to learning activities and began working with an animal-drawn cart, hauling goods to bring in money. With his mother dead and his father badly injured, OCHA writes, he had taken on an adult's share of responsibility for meeting the family's basic needs at an age when he should have been in a classroom.

It was his sister who asked for help. A protection team run by DanChurchAid and its local partner, the MA'AN Development Center, assessed the household and drew up a plan for the whole family. Shadi received individual counselling and psychosocial support, and was referred for speech therapy, for help with his visual impairment and for a place in a learning programme. The family was linked to food assistance and health care to ease the financial pressure that had pushed him into work.

Over time, the account says, Shadi grew more comfortable in the sessions and started to look forward to them. He told the team that he feels very comfortable and waits for the sessions every day. With continued case management for him and his relatives, he has gone back to school. His sister said the family had learned things it did not know before, and that the support they received had changed both of them.

The project is financed by the occupied Palestinian territory Humanitarian Fund and serves more than 15,000 people in Khan Younis and Deir al-Balah through community-based counselling, psychosocial support and referrals. OCHA sets Shadi's case against wider figures: tens of thousands of children in Gaza have been injured over the past three years, UNICEF estimates that tens of thousands have lost one or both parents, and about 60 per cent of school-age children had no in-person learning in the 2024-2025 school year.

Getting children back into class is a system-wide effort. In the week to 2 November, education partners sent 164,530 school bags to 385 learning spaces, OCHA reported. The storm that followed damaged 20 of those spaces and pushed attendance at others as low as 3 per cent. The agency's authors are careful about what protection work can do: it cannot undo a child's losses, they write, but it can restore routine and a way back to learning.

subheads.2: A plan for the whole family
