stories.title: What happened during Israel's ten-day operation in Hebron, and what did families find when it ended?
stories.short: What happened in Hebron's ten-day lockdown?
stories.gist: From 23 October to 2 November Israeli forces sealed two Hebron neighbourhoods, displacing more than 3,000 people who are now returning.
body: It began with a shooting. On Friday 23 October two Palestinian gunmen opened fire on an Israeli military checkpoint at the edge of Hebron, killing two soldiers and wounding several others before being shot dead. Within hours Israeli forces had sealed the Jildah and Ein Deir Bahah neighbourhoods and imposed sweeping movement restrictions on the city and its surroundings. The operation lasted ten days and ended on 2 November, according to OCHA.

Counts of the displaced rose through the week. The UN said on 26 October that more than 3,000 people had been evacuated by Israeli forces. On 29 October Hebron governor Khaled Dudin put the figure at 537 families, or 3,361 people, among them 232 infants, 326 older people and 147 pregnant or breastfeeding women. By 30 October WAFA reported about 5,000 people either displaced or confined to their homes. OCHA notes that the municipality's figures are still being verified.

Daily life stopped well beyond the two neighbourhoods. OCHA says about 90,000 students in the Hebron education directorate were affected by a temporary suspension of in-person teaching, and 11 schools with some 4,450 pupils remained out of reach until 3 November. The Hebron Chamber of Commerce estimated losses of 10 to 12 million shekels a day. Palestinian sources reported more than 115 arrests; WAFA described a protest by displaced families at the closed Jildah roundabout on 30 October.

On 30 October Israeli forces used explosives to demolish two apartments belonging to the families of the two attackers. OCHA says three families, 15 people including nine children, lost their homes, neighbouring flats were damaged and eight relatives were arrested. Such punitive demolitions accounted for seven of the 31 Palestinian-owned structures destroyed across the West Bank during that week, the office said.

The UN's human rights chief, Volker Türk, said on 26 October that the operation raised grave concerns of unnecessary and disproportionate force and that collective punishment is a grave violation of international law. He said threats by senior officials to empty neighbourhoods raised serious concerns of ethnic cleansing. Sixty members of the European Parliament wrote to the EU's foreign policy chief calling the closure collective punishment. Israel said it was acting against those behind a deadly attack.

Families started going back after 2 November. OCHA reports damage to belongings, including in homes that had reportedly been used as military positions. Aid agencies and the municipality have given one round of emergency cash, about 500 food parcels, blankets, mattresses and hygiene kits, and a second cash round is being considered. Mobile clinics were still suspended in 10 places in the governorate on 3 November. A delegation of UN and NGO heads visited the city the day the operation ended.

photo.caption: Archive: view over part of Hebron's Old City, May 2022. The neighbourhoods sealed in October lie elsewhere in the city.

stories.title: Greece commits €600,000 to East Jerusalem hospitals as WHO data show a quarter of patient permits unmet
stories.short: Greece gives €600,000 to East Jerusalem hospitals
stories.gist: Greece signed a €600,000 grant for East Jerusalem hospitals on 2 November; WHO says 76% of patient permit requests were approved this year.
body: Greece has committed €600,000 to the hospitals of East Jerusalem. The agreement was signed on Monday 2 November by the Greek consul general in Jerusalem, Dimitrios Angelosopoulos, and the Palestinian Authority's minister of finance and planning, Estephan Salameh, WAFA reported. The money will be paid through PEGASE, the direct financial support mechanism set up by the European Commission and run by the office of the EU representative in Jerusalem.

The East Jerusalem hospitals are a network of Palestinian charitable and church-run institutions, among them Augusta Victoria on the Mount of Olives and Makassed, that provide specialised treatment not available elsewhere in the Palestinian health system. They treat patients referred from across the West Bank and Gaza by the Palestinian Authority, which is why donor support for them is routed through an agreement with the authority's finance ministry. WAFA described the Greek money as a contribution to essential health care services.

Getting to the hospitals is its own obstacle. Patients from the rest of the West Bank and from Gaza need an Israeli permit to enter East Jerusalem. The World Health Organization reports that 76 per cent of 93,051 patient permit applications for treatment in East Jerusalem or Israel were approved between January and October 2026, according to OCHA. That is an improvement on 64 per cent in 2025 but still below the level before October 2023.

The remaining quarter matters, the UN office notes, because applications that were denied or still pending were not resolved by the date of the patient's appointment. A permit that arrives after the appointment date is, in practice, a missed treatment session or a postponed operation, whatever the eventual decision. OCHA adds that 872 health service points were functioning across the West Bank in October, 490 of them only partially.

The road in is slow even with a permit. On the evening of 1 November WAFA reported long queues at the Qalandia checkpoint and the nearby roundabout in Kafr Aqab, and at the Shu'fat refugee camp checkpoint, after Israeli forces tightened procedures, and a temporary checkpoint at the entrance to Hizma. On 9 November the entrances to Hizma were closed altogether.

Greece is not alone in directing money at Palestinian health care this month. Japan signed a $1.97 million grant with the WHO on 10 November for emergency medical coordination in Gaza, and Arab health ministers meeting the same day called for continued support to the Palestinian health sector. For the Jerusalem hospitals the Greek contribution is modest in scale, but it arrives at a moment when UN agencies report that funding for health and relief work is shrinking.

photo.caption: Archive: the Augusta Victoria Hospital compound on the Mount of Olives, East Jerusalem, January 2025.

stories.title: What was the Balfour Declaration, and why do Palestinians still mark its anniversary 109 years on?
stories.short: What was the Balfour Declaration?
stories.gist: A 1917 letter in which Britain backed a 'national home for the Jewish people' in Palestine; Palestinians date their dispossession from it.
body: The Balfour Declaration was a letter. On 2 November 1917 the British foreign secretary, Arthur James Balfour, wrote to Lord Rothschild, a leading figure in the Zionist movement, to say that the British government viewed with favour the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people. The operative text was a single sentence. Monday 2 November was its 109th anniversary, which the Palestinian news agency WAFA marked with a long retrospective.

The letter followed about three years of contacts between the British government and Zionist representatives, who argued that their project could serve British strategic interests in the region. Before it was made public, London sought the approval of the US president, Woodrow Wilson. France and Italy endorsed it in 1918. At the time Palestine was still part of the Ottoman Empire, and British troops were only then advancing into it.

What turned a letter into policy was the mandate system. In 1920 the Allied powers, meeting at San Remo, awarded Britain the mandate for Palestine and charged it with putting the declaration into effect. The League of Nations approved the mandate in July 1922 and it came into force in September 1923. WAFA's account stresses that this made the declaration a commitment of the Western powers as a whole, not of Britain alone.

The text mentioned the people already living in Palestine only as existing non-Jewish communities whose civil and religious rights should not be prejudiced. It said nothing of their political rights. That omission is at the centre of the Palestinian objection: a foreign power promised a national home in a country it did not yet control to a movement based largely outside it, without consulting the population that lived there.

Opposition was immediate in the Arab world, and Britain tried to reassure Sharif Hussein of Mecca that Jewish settlement would not go beyond what was compatible with Arab interests. On the ground, immigration was facilitated under the mandate. Palestinians responded with protests and uprisings, among them the Buraq uprising of 1929 and the revolt that began in 1936. Israel was established in May 1948, and hundreds of thousands of Palestinians were displaced.

The anniversary remains a fixed date in the Palestinian calendar, marked each year by official statements and by commentary of the kind WAFA published this week. Britain's own position has shifted over the decades: it recognised the State of Palestine in September 2025. In the retrospective's closing words, the declaration was a promise made by a foreign power in a land already inhabited by another people, whose rights and aspirations were left out of the equation.

photo.caption: Archive: Lord Allenby, Lord Balfour and Sir Herbert Samuel during Balfour's visit to Jerusalem, 1 April 1925.

stories.title: What is the 'yellow line' in Gaza, and why does the UN say people near it keep being displaced?
stories.short: What is Gaza's 'yellow line'?
stories.gist: It is the line Israeli forces pulled back to under the October 2025 ceasefire; the UN says it is shifting west and treated as a kill zone.
body: The yellow line is the boundary to which Israeli forces withdrew under the ceasefire agreement of October 2025. East of it the army remains deployed; west of it is the shrinking strip where most of Gaza's population now lives. The UN humanitarian office has described the line as largely unmarked on the ground, although its latest reports mention new yellow concrete blocks appearing in Ash Shuja'iyyeh and in parts of Deir al-Balah.

The UN human rights office says the line is moving. In a statement on 30 October it reported that Israel has declared an aim of expanding its military deployment area to 70 per cent of Gaza's territory, and that over the previous two weeks its monitors documented westward expansion in Shuja'iyyeh and Gaza City and at three points in central Gaza: eastern Al Bureij, eastern Deir al-Balah and eastern Al Maghazi.

For families camped nearby, that means moving again. The office said it received reports that on 25 October a drone dropped munitions on tents at Shuja'iyyeh junction, starting a fire that burned for five hours. The Palestinian Ministry of Public Works and Housing said 200 families, about 800 people, were displaced. UN teams who visited the area days later found that more tents had been set alight, leaving at least nine households without shelter.

Ajith Sunghay, who heads the UN human rights office in the occupied Palestinian territory, called displacement in Gaza both acute and chronic. People uprooted before the ceasefire have little prospect of going home, he said, because most of their neighbourhoods lie beyond the line. His office said Israeli forces appear to treat the line as a kill zone, and that forcible transfer within occupied territory is a war crime.

An independent UN Commission of Inquiry reached a similar conclusion in a report presented to the General Assembly on 26 October. Its chair, Srinivasan Muralidhar, said Israel's expansion of territorial control continues to result in the killing and harming of Palestinians who approach or cross the line. Israel rejected the commission's findings; its mission in Geneva called the report part of a misinformation campaign to demonise the state.

The Gaza Ministry of Health counted 36 people killed and 145 injured between 27 October and 2 November, and 1,593 killed since the ceasefire took effect, according to OCHA. UN staff have been caught up too: the organisation reported shooting near three UN schools and a convoy in late October, and said staff had to take cover from gunfire west of the line in Gaza City on 7 November.

photo.caption: Archive: a street in central Gaza City lined with destroyed buildings, February 2025.

stories.title: Bethlehem tenth-grader Ghazal Taim takes second place among 40 million in the Arab Reading Challenge
stories.short: Bethlehem pupil is runner-up in Arab Reading Challenge
stories.gist: Ghazal Taim, 16, of al-Awda Secondary School for Girls, finished second in the 10th Arab Reading Challenge final in Dubai on 29 October.
body: A 16-year-old from the Bethlehem area has finished second in the Arab world's biggest reading competition. Ghazal Rashad Adel Taim, a tenth-grade pupil at al-Awda Secondary School for Girls, was named runner-up in the 10th Arab Reading Challenge at a closing ceremony at the Dubai World Trade Centre on Thursday 29 October, WAFA reported. She had travelled to the final as Palestine's national champion.

Six finalists competed in front of a live audience. Each was given one minute to answer a direct question, after which those attending voted for the winner. First place went to 11-year-old Mayar al-Shorbagy of Egypt, and third to Rayan al-Sukari of Saudi Arabia. The ceremony was attended by Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, the ruler of Dubai and vice-president of the United Arab Emirates.

Getting to Dubai meant winning at home first. The Palestinian round drew 712,765 pupils from 1,719 schools, supervised by 4,788 coordinators, according to the figures published with the result. Those numbers include schools in a year when classes have been repeatedly interrupted: in late October alone, about 90,000 pupils in the neighbouring Hebron directorate lost days of in-person teaching during an Israeli military operation, the UN reported.

The challenge is a reading competition in Arabic in which pupils advance from their own schools to a national title and then to the regional final, as Taim did after winning the Palestinian round. The organisers, the Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum Global Initiatives foundation, launched it in 2015 to encourage reading and strengthen the place of Arabic among younger generations. This year's tenth edition was the largest so far.

In all, 40,286,428 pupils from 60 countries took part, 24 per cent more than in the ninth edition, and 138,426 schools were involved under 161,507 coordinators. The organisers said 74,062 of the participants were pupils with disabilities. Against that field, second place puts a girl from a school in the Bethlehem education directorate ahead of all but one of roughly 40 million readers.

Young Palestinians have also been collecting results elsewhere this autumn. WAFA reported on 19 October that the national kickboxing team returned from a World Cup in Tashkent with two gold and six bronze medals. The contrast with Gaza is stark: OCHA notes that about 60 per cent of school-age children there had no in-person learning in the 2024-2025 school year, and aid agencies were still distributing school bags to temporary learning spaces this month.

photo.caption: Archive: Manger Square and the Mosque of Omar in central Bethlehem, April 2012.

stories.title: What does the UN rapporteur's new report say about the killing and jailing of Palestinian journalists?
stories.short: What does the UN report on Palestinian journalists say?
stories.gist: Francesca Albanese's report says nearly 300 journalists and media workers have been killed in Gaza and 80% of its media offices destroyed.
body: The UN special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory, Francesca Albanese, presented a report on the media to journalists on Tuesday 27 October. Titled 'Truth under the rubble: media in the time of genocide', it was submitted to the General Assembly. She briefed reporters by video link because US sanctions imposed on her prevent her from travelling to New York. Special rapporteurs are independent experts appointed by the Human Rights Council and do not speak for the UN.

Her central figures concern Gaza. Citing UN sources, Albanese said nearly 300 journalists and media workers have been killed there since October 2023, more than 100 have been detained, many of them tortured, and about 150 media centres and offices have been destroyed, which she put at 80 per cent of Gaza's media infrastructure. A statement by a group of UN experts on 2 November added that more than 400 have been wounded.

The report identifies around 70 journalists who, it alleges, were killed in reprisal for their work, the experts' statement said. It calls for independent, prompt and effective investigations and for journalists' material to be preserved as potential evidence. Israel has denied targeting journalists as such. Counting is itself contested: in September the Committee to Protect Journalists removed 22 names from its list of journalists killed in Gaza after they were identified as militants, according to a chronology of the year's events.

The West Bank receives its own chapter. Albanese said more than 139 attacks on journalists have recently been recorded there. Reporters covering this autumn's olive harvest have been among those affected: two foreign journalists were among 17 people detained by Israeli forces in Kafr Ni'ma on 6 November, WAFA reported, and a journalist was injured in a settler attack south of Nablus on 10 November.

Albanese criticised Israel's continuing ban on foreign journalists entering Gaza independently, which leaves coverage dependent on local reporters. She also raised the case of Shireen Abu Akleh, the Al Jazeera correspondent shot dead in Jenin in May 2022, for whose killing no one has been held to account. Asked for an update on accountability, she answered that the update is impunity.

The report is not limited to Israel. It documents intimidation and repression of Palestinian journalists by Hamas in Gaza and by the Palestinian Authority in the West Bank. The wider context was set out by the UN experts on the international day against impunity for crimes against journalists: according to UNESCO, more than 1,800 journalists were killed worldwide between 2006 and 2025, and close to nine in ten of those killings remain unresolved in court.

photo.credit: Al Jazeera Media Network / Wikimedia Commons
photo.caption: Archive: Shireen Abu Akleh, the Al Jazeera correspondent killed in Jenin in May 2022, in an undated photograph released by the network.

stories.title: Israel turns back 23 foreign parliamentarians and academics bound for Birzeit University conference
stories.short: Israel bars 23-member delegation from Birzeit conference
stories.gist: A delegation including British MP Clive Lewis was questioned for hours at the Allenby crossing on 27 October and refused entry.
body: Israeli authorities refused entry to the West Bank on Tuesday 27 October to an international delegation of 23 parliamentarians, politicians and academics who were travelling to a conference at Birzeit University, the university said. The group arrived at the Allenby crossing, the land crossing between Jordan and the West Bank, which Israel controls. According to the organisers, its members were held and questioned for several hours before being turned back.

Birzeit named several of those refused entry: the British Labour MP Clive Lewis; Lara Bird of the Scottish National Party; Kate Nevens, a Scottish Green member of the Scottish Parliament; the Spanish senator Josu Estarrona Elizondo of EH Bildu; and the former British MP Sam Tarry. The full delegation came from several countries, the university's statement said, without listing every name.

They had been invited to a conference organised by the university's Ibrahim Abu-Lughod Institute of International Studies under the title 'Global South Solidarity and Resistance to Imperialism', which opened the same day. Their programme also included meetings with students, academics and civil society organisations, and joining activities in support of farmers during the olive harvest, at a time of escalating settler attacks.

The date was not incidental. Israel had imposed a full closure on the West Bank after a deadly shooting near Hebron four days earlier, and 27 October was election day in Israel. There was no statement from the Israeli authorities on the reasons for the refusal in the reports available. Israel controls all entry to the West Bank and has in recent years denied entry to a number of foreign politicians critical of its policies.

The university said the refusal fits a pattern of restrictions on Palestinian academic institutions and on their contact with scholars, parliamentarians and delegations from abroad. Such restrictions, it said, obstruct academic exchange and prevent visitors from seeing conditions under occupation for themselves. It called for the protection of academic freedom and of universities' ability to work with partners and supporters internationally.

The conference was due to open the same day. The previous evening, 60 members of the European Parliament had sent a letter calling for EU sanctions over the Hebron closure, and on 6 November Israel ordered the deportation of 12 foreign volunteers detained while helping with the olive harvest near Ramallah. Birzeit, north of Ramallah, is one of the oldest Palestinian universities.

photo.caption: Archive: a lecture for a visiting foreign delegation at Birzeit University, June 2023.

stories.title: Sixty members of the European Parliament urge emergency EU meeting on sanctions over Hebron closure
stories.short: 60 MEPs press EU for sanctions over Hebron closure
stories.gist: In a letter to EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas, 60 MEPs called the West Bank closure collective punishment and asked for sanctions talks.
body: Sixty members of the European Parliament have asked the EU's foreign policy chief, Kaja Kallas, to convene an urgent meeting of the bloc's foreign ministers to agree sanctions on the Israeli government. The request came in a letter sent on the evening of Monday 26 October and signed by lawmakers from several of the parliament's political groups, WAFA reported the following day.

The trigger was the closure imposed on the West Bank after two Israeli soldiers were shot dead at a checkpoint near Hebron on 23 October. The letter describes the measures as collective punishment, which it says constitutes a war crime under international law, and accuses the Israeli government of using them to consolidate its occupation and to raise tensions during Israel's election campaign. Polling day was 27 October.

The signatories cite the demolition of homes in Hebron and say some families were given no more than five minutes to leave. They call the events a decisive turning point for the future of the West Bank and for the viability of a Palestinian state, and say the European Union cannot remain silent in the face of what they describe as a large-scale assault.

Their demands are threefold: that the EU condemn the measures, that it call for the withdrawal of Israeli forces from the West Bank, and that foreign ministers meet urgently to reach agreement on sanctions. Sanctions require unanimity among the 27 member states, which is why the letter asks for a ministerial meeting and not for a decision by Kallas herself.

By the time the letter was sent, according to figures from Hebron officials quoted by WAFA, 619 families had been affected by the operation, about 3,971 people had been displaced and 85 arrested. The UN human rights chief, Volker Türk, said the same day that the operation raised grave concerns of disproportionate force and that collective punishment is a grave violation of international law.

The EU has not announced such a meeting. On 10 November it repeated its demand that Israel ensure the delivery of humanitarian aid to Gaza, WAFA reported. Other governments have moved separately: the British foreign secretary said in October that the UK had created powers to sanction companies involved in building settlements in the E1 area, and twelve countries announced restrictions on settlement products in September, according to a chronology of the year.

photo.caption: Archive: the European Parliament's chamber in Strasbourg, June 2021.

stories.title: What did the UN Commission of Inquiry conclude in its October report on the West Bank and Gaza?
stories.short: What did the UN inquiry's October report find?
stories.gist: The commission found war crimes and crimes against humanity in the West Bank and said genocidal acts continue in Gaza; Israel rejects this.
body: The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel presented its latest report to the UN General Assembly on Monday 26 October. Its headline finding is that Israel has committed war crimes and the crimes against humanity of extermination, persecution, torture, rape and other forms of sexual violence against Palestinians, and that it continues to commit genocide in Gaza after the ceasefire of October 2025.

The commission was set up by the UN Human Rights Council in 2021 and is chaired by Srinivasan Muralidhar. Its members are independent experts; they are not UN staff and are not paid for the work. This report concentrates on killings and on bodily and mental harm attributed to state actors, and devotes most of its new material to the West Bank.

There, the commission says, the situation has deteriorated gravely since 7 October 2023. One of its statistics concerns air power: six Palestinians were killed by air strikes in the West Bank between 2008 and 6 October 2023, and 254 between 7 October 2023 and 30 September 2026. It concludes that military operations and sustained settler violence together amount to a widespread and systematic attack on civilians, and that the authorities intended them to work in concert.

The report describes military operations since January 2025 as having caused the largest displacement of Palestinians in the West Bank since 1967, with 34,176 people still displaced in August 2026. It finds that children have been deliberately killed and harmed, which it classes as persecution on grounds of age, and that sexual violence has been used to displace and subjugate.

On Gaza, the commission says Israeli authorities and forces have continued to commit genocidal acts since the ceasefire, with intent to destroy Palestinians in whole or in part, and that the expansion of Israeli territorial control results in the killing of people who approach or cross the so-called yellow line. Muralidhar said the pattern forms part of a broader strategy to displace Palestinians and impose unliveable conditions.

Israel rejected the report. Its permanent mission in Geneva called it yet another manifestation of a misinformation campaign to demonise the State of Israel. Israel does not cooperate with the commission and has long accused it of bias. The commission's findings are not binding; it recommends that Israel comply with the International Court of Justice's advisory opinion of July 2024, end the occupation, remove settlements and return confiscated land to its owners.

photo.caption: Archive: the Human Rights and Alliance of Civilizations Room at the UN in Geneva, where the Human Rights Council meets, August 2015.

stories.title: Ben-Gvir enters Al-Aqsa compound on the eve of Israel's election, drawing protests from Cairo and Doha
stories.short: Ben-Gvir at Al-Aqsa on election eve; Egypt, Qatar protest
stories.gist: Israel's national security minister entered the Al-Aqsa compound under guard on 26 October, a day before the vote; Egypt and Qatar condemned it.
body: Israel's national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, entered the Al-Aqsa Mosque compound in Jerusalem's Old City under heavy police guard on Monday 26 October, the day before Israel's parliamentary election. The Palestinian Authority's Jerusalem Governorate said he was accompanied by the Knesset member Moshe Feiglin. It was his third reported entry in two months, after visits on 31 August and on 28 September, when he came with the defence minister, Israel Katz, during the Jewish festival of Sukkot.

The compound, known to Jews as the Temple Mount, is administered by a Jordanian-backed Islamic trust under an arrangement usually called the status quo: non-Muslims may visit at set times but only Muslims may pray there. Ben-Gvir has said openly that he wants Jewish prayer on the site expanded. Palestinians, and the governments that responded on Monday, see each visit as a step towards changing that arrangement.

Egypt's foreign ministry condemned the entry, which it said took place alongside hundreds of settlers and under police protection, as a flagrant violation of the sanctity of Islamic holy sites and of the historical and legal status quo in East Jerusalem. Cairo said it rejected any attempt to divide the mosque by time or by space and called on other governments to act.

Qatar's foreign ministry called the visit an unacceptable provocation to Muslims around the world and said all unilateral measures aimed at altering the status of Jerusalem and its holy places are void under international law. Both statements were carried by WAFA. The timing, hours before polls opened, was noted in Palestinian commentary as part of a campaign in which right-wing parties competed over hard-line positions.

The election changed the political picture around the minister. On 8 November President Isaac Herzog formally asked Gadi Eizenkot, leader of the Yashar party, to form a government after he was recommended by 67 members of the Knesset against 46 for Benjamin Netanyahu, WAFA reported. Coalition talks are continuing, and the present government, including Ben-Gvir, remains in office in a caretaker capacity until a new one is sworn in.

Entries by groups of religious nationalist Israelis have continued in the meantime. On the morning of Tuesday 10 November, local sources told WAFA, dozens entered through the Mughrabi Gate under police protection and performed religious rituals in the eastern part of the compound, near the Dome of the Rock. Egypt had issued a further condemnation of such entries two days earlier.

stories.title: Palestinian Women's Day in numbers: what official statistics say about 2.75 million women and girls
stories.short: Palestinian Women's Day, in seven numbers
stories.gist: For Women's Day on 26 October, the statistics bureau reported that women head about a quarter of Gaza's households and 28,560 are widowed.
body: 2.75 million. That is the number of women and girls in Palestine at the end of 2025, about 49 per cent of the population, according to figures released for Palestinian Women's Day on 26 October by the Palestinian Central Bureau of Statistics and the Ministry of Women's Affairs. Of these, 1.69 million live in the West Bank and 1.06 million in Gaza. The joint release sets out what three years of war have done to their lives.

12,500. More than this many women have been killed in Gaza since October 2023, among 74,382 deaths recorded by the Ministry of Health up to 12 October 2026, the release says. More than 9,000 of them were mothers, and 42 were journalists. Women account for about 14 per cent of the 175,416 people recorded as injured. In the West Bank, 28 women are among 1,216 Palestinians killed in the same period.

28,560. That many women in Gaza have been widowed by the war. The share of households headed by a woman rose from 12 per cent before the war to about 18 per cent by October 2025. UN Women data for 2026, cited in the release, put the number of female-headed households at about 86,290, nearly a quarter of all households in Gaza once women whose husbands are missing, detained or severely injured are included.

50,000. An estimated 50,000 women in Gaza are pregnant, with up to 180 births a day, while about 94 per cent of health facilities have been damaged or destroyed. In the first half of 2026, the release says, more than 3,950 pregnancy losses were recorded, 57.1 per cent of pregnant women were anaemic and 49.2 per cent of births were by caesarean section. About 24,600 pregnant and breastfeeding women are acutely malnourished.

5.9. The death rate among women of reproductive age in Gaza reached 5.9 per 1,000 in 2025, against 0.7 per 1,000 in 2022. The figure comes from the same release and is the starkest single measure in it: an eightfold increase in three years among women aged roughly 15 to 49, which the bureau attributes to the collapse of health and living conditions.

87. That was the number of women in Israeli prisons on 12 October, 21 of them held in administrative detention without charge, out of about 9,300 Palestinian detainees. Prisoners' organisations count 800 women among more than 26,000 arrests in the West Bank since October 2023. By 10 November the Palestinian detainees' commission put the number of women held at 90, three of them minors.

2,400. In the West Bank, the release says, demolitions and confiscations of more than 4,750 structures between October 2023 and September 2026 displaced over 8,660 people, of whom 2,400 were women and about 3,700 children. The ministry's conclusion is about policy as much as loss: it wants women involved in setting priorities for relief and reconstruction. In May it launched a national observatory to monitor violence against women.

stories.title: Jerusalem Governorate says tunnelling under Silwan is cracking homes and rewriting the area's history
stories.short: Governorate: tunnels under Silwan are cracking homes
stories.gist: The Palestinian Jerusalem Governorate says excavations beneath Wadi Hilweh have caused cracks and collapses and serve a selective narrative.
body: Excavations and tunnel construction are continuing beneath Silwan, the Palestinian neighbourhood just south of the Old City walls, and are putting homes at risk, the Palestinian Authority's Jerusalem Governorate said in a statement on 25 October. It singled out the Wadi Hilweh area, where Israeli authorities and settler organisations have dug for years under and between houses, and where an archaeological park run by a settler group draws large numbers of visitors.

The governorate said reports have documented cracks, partial collapses and structural damage in houses above the excavation sites. It framed the issue as one of safety and of residents' ability to stay in their homes, rather than of heritage alone. The statement did not give a figure for the number of buildings affected, and the claims could not be checked independently.

Its second complaint concerns method. The governorate said the bodies directing the digs choose where to excavate in order to support a particular historical narrative, concentrating on layers associated with the 10th century BCE while giving little attention to other periods that reflect the succession of civilisations in Jerusalem. Finds are tied to biblical accounts and sites are given biblical names, it said.

In the governorate's words, that turns archaeology from a scientific effort to understand the city's past across different eras into a tool for advancing a political narrative and justifying the takeover of land. The WAFA report that carried the statement did not include a response from the Israeli authorities or from the organisations that run the excavations, and none was available at the time of writing.

The works are spread across what planners call the Holy Basin, the area between the Old City and the Mount of Olives. The governorate listed the neighbourhoods of Silwan, Wadi Hilweh, al-Bustan and Wadi al-Rababa and said the projects reach north towards Sheikh Jarrah. Several of them, al-Bustan in particular, have also seen Palestinian homes demolished in recent weeks, the governorate says.

Above ground, the same streets saw two demolitions in the days after the statement. On 28 October a resident of Silwan's Ein al-Lawza area was made to demolish his own house, and on 4 November bulldozers destroyed an 80-square-metre house in al-Bustan that had stood for 25 years, damaging roads and uprooting trees to reach it, the governorate said. Its owner, Suleiman Abu Subaih, lived there with his wife.

stories.title: New international volume documents the fate of Palestinian libraries and archives from 1948 to 1993
stories.short: New book traces the history of Palestinian libraries
stories.gist: 'Resisting Erasure', from Library Juice Press, includes Anan Hamad's study of Palestinian libraries and archives under occupation, 1948-1993.
body: A new book from the international publisher Library Juice Press sets out to document what has happened to Palestinian libraries and archives over the past three quarters of a century. 'Resisting Erasure: Libraries in Palestine and Palestine in Libraries' includes a full-length study by the Palestinian researcher Anan Hamad, 'History of Palestinian Libraries and Archives Under Israeli Occupation (1948-1993)', WAFA reported on 19 October.

Hamad's study follows libraries and archival collections from their origins through the decades after 1948, up to the year of the Oslo accords. It examines how they were founded and developed, the obstacles they faced under Israeli occupation, and the targeting and looting of major intellectual and archival collections, according to the agency's description of the work. It covers 45 years in all.

The volume as a whole looks in two directions, as its title suggests: at libraries inside Palestine, and at how Palestine is represented, catalogued and collected in libraries elsewhere. For researchers abroad and for Palestinians in the diaspora who depend on foreign collections to study their own history, the second question is as practical as the first, because it decides what can be found.

WAFA describes the study as a contribution to documenting national memory and preserving cultural and intellectual heritage, and as a reference for future generations of researchers interested in the country's history. Including it in full in an English-language academic book, the agency notes, places Palestinian knowledge resources before an international readership that might not otherwise encounter research by Palestinian scholars.

The book appears at a time of heavy losses to cultural institutions. The UN's special rapporteur on the occupied Palestinian territory, Francesca Albanese, told reporters on 27 October that about 150 media centres and offices in Gaza have been destroyed, some 80 per cent of the territory's media infrastructure. The Palestinian delegate to UNESCO told its executive board in October that education and culture in Gaza had been hit across the organisation's whole mandate.

Interest in the field is growing in universities. On the day the book was announced, the University of Barcelona launched Spain's first chair in Palestine studies, with research on heritage among its stated aims. Hamad's history ends in 1993; the story of what has happened to Palestinian libraries, archives and their catalogues since then, including during the past three years in Gaza, is still being written.

stories.title: Palestinian kickboxers bring home two golds and six bronzes from the World Cup in Tashkent
stories.short: Palestinian kickboxers win eight medals in Tashkent
stories.gist: Abdullah Kanaan and Mohammad Alyan won gold as Palestine's 27-strong team took eight medals at the kickboxing World Cup in Uzbekistan.
body: Palestine's kickboxing team finished the World Cup for national teams and clubs in Tashkent with two gold medals and six bronze, WAFA reported on 19 October. The tournament in the Uzbek capital brought together around 3,000 athletes from 77 teams. Abdullah Kanaan won gold in the senior category and Mohammad Alyan took gold among the juniors, giving the team a title at each level.

The six bronze medals went to Mustafa Sharaf, Anas al-Qaq, Mohammad Oweisat, Ahmad Sbeih, Yahya Jabr and Waad Bkeirat. The delegation numbered 27 male and female athletes and was led by Nizar Taleb, vice-president of the Palestinian Kickboxing Federation, with federation board members Tamer Bakr and Wasim Shamlawi on the administrative staff. WAFA did not list the weight classes in which the medals were won.

The squad was drawn from seven clubs and training centres, a list that reads like a map of the West Bank and Jerusalem: Aswar Beit al-Maqdis Club, the Al-Bustan Silwan Association, Be Strong Gym, Silwad Sports Club, Meithalun Sports Club, the Champions Center for Martial Arts and Target One MMA. Silwad lies north-east of Ramallah and Meithalun south of Jenin; al-Bustan is a neighbourhood of Silwan, in East Jerusalem.

Palestine's ambassador to Uzbekistan, Wael al-Batrikhi, congratulated the federation and put the result in the context of the year. Across five international competitions in 2026, he said, the national team has won 17 gold, 18 silver and 14 bronze medals. The federation says taking part in such events is part of a plan to develop the national squads and raise Palestine's presence in international sport.

It was a good week for Palestinian combat sports. On 18 October Maryam Bsharat won gold in the junior women's under-66kg kumite at the World Cadet, Junior and Under-21 Karate Championships in Poland, according to a chronology of the year's events. The two results came within twenty-four hours of each other, on different continents, in two different martial arts and at two different age levels.

The clubs behind the medals work in difficult conditions. Less than three weeks later, on 5 November, Israeli authorities closed the Sons of Jerusalem Club, a sports and social club in the Old City, by ministerial order, and on 10 November police renewed the closure of the Burj al-Laqlaq youth centre for six months. The Palestinian Authority's Jerusalem Governorate described both steps as narrowing the space for sport in the city.

stories.title: University of Barcelona launches Spain's first academic chair dedicated to Palestine studies
stories.short: Barcelona launches Spain's first Palestine studies chair
stories.gist: The UB-Fundacions Ferrer Chair for Palestine Studies was inaugurated in Barcelona with An-Najah's Sanaa Alsarghali taking part.
body: The University of Barcelona has inaugurated what it describes as the first academic chair in Spain devoted to Palestine studies. The UB-Fundacions Ferrer Chair for Palestine Studies was launched in cooperation with the Fundacions Ferrer group of foundations, WAFA reported on 19 October. The university's rector, Professor Joan Guàrdia, attended the ceremony alongside Palestine's ambassador to Spain, Fadi al-Husseini, the agency said in a dispatch from Barcelona.

The chair is intended to promote Palestine studies in European universities and to support interdisciplinary research on Palestinian history, society, culture and heritage as well as political and legal questions. Guàrdia spoke at the ceremony about the part universities play in advancing knowledge and human rights, and about widening academic cooperation with Palestinian institutions, according to the agency's account of the event.

Dr Sanaa Alsarghali took part in the launch. She is an associate professor of constitutional law at An-Najah National University in Nablus and holds the UNESCO Chair for Human Rights, Democracy and Peace there. She stressed the importance of cooperation between Palestinian and European universities, of support for Palestinian research, and of raising the international profile of Palestinian scholarship and identity.

Alsarghali also drew attention to the conditions under which Palestinian higher education operates and argued that international partnerships are one of the ways to sustain it. The difficulties are practical as well as financial. On 27 October Israeli authorities turned back a 23-member international delegation of parliamentarians and academics at the Allenby crossing as it travelled to a conference at Birzeit University, the university said.

The Barcelona chair arrives as international bodies pay closer attention to Palestinian education. WAFA reported the same day that UNESCO's executive board, meeting in Paris for its 225th session, had unanimously adopted two resolutions: one on the effects of the situation in Gaza on education, science and culture, and one supporting the continuation of schooling provided by the UN agency for Palestine refugees.

Spain recognised the State of Palestine in 2024, and the ambassador's presence at the ceremony gave the launch a diplomatic as well as an academic character. For Palestinians living in Catalonia and for Spanish students, a university chair offers something more durable than a single conference or exhibition: a standing programme whose purpose is to teach, research and publish on Palestine from one academic year to the next.
